soil-env-144.title: Ice Age life waiting in the frozen ground
soil-env-144.text: In 2012 Russian researchers brought a plant back to life from tissue 30,000 years old. They found it in an Ice Age squirrel burrow sealed in frozen ground and grew Silene stenophylla, the oldest plant tissue ever revived. Permafrost also holds dormant bacteria and inactive viruses. Some scientists worry that thaw could free unknown pathogens of humans, livestock or crops. Others note that pathogens such as influenza and smallpox seem unable to survive thawing, and a scientific review rates the risk as generally low. The question is still argued.

soil-env-132.title: Subsea permafrost, the Ice Age land the sea drowned
soil-env-132.text: Some permafrost lies under the sea. Subsea permafrost sits beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves. It froze on dry land during the last Ice Age, when sea levels were low, and the rising sea later flooded it. Warmer, saltier conditions have slowly shrunk it ever since. Today it covers an estimated 2 million km2, about a fifth of the land permafrost domain and 30–50% less than at the Last Glacial Maximum. It holds around 560 GtC in organic matter and 45 GtC as methane, and releases 18 and 38 MtC a year as it still responds to post-glacial warming. Under the RCP 8.5 scenario it could release 43 GtC by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300. Yet the effects of human-driven warming will show there only after hundreds or thousands of years.

soil-env-141.title: Drunken trees and sliding slopes on thawing ground
soil-env-141.text: Trees tilting at random, so-called drunken trees, are a sure sign that the ground beneath them is thawing. As permafrost ice melts and the water drains or evaporates, soil structure weakens and can turn viscous. Warming has increased slope disturbances on permafrost, sharply raising the sediment that rivers carry, and thaw can also drain and dry northern wetlands. In high mountains, thaw builds pore-water pressure and lowers slope stability, leading to slope failures and rockfalls such as the 1987 Val Pola landslide. Thaw also forms frozen debris lobes, slow landslides of soil, rock, trees and ice. By December 2021, 43 had been identified in Alaska's southern Brooks Range.

soil-env-120.title: The root fungi that hold much of the soil's carbon
soil-env-120.text: On forested islands in Sweden, fungi living on tree roots hold 50 to 70 percent of the carbon stored in leaf litter and soil. These are the mycorrhizal fungi of {{ref:soil-bio-157}}, partners of the roots of almost all plants. Alongside plants, decomposers and minerals, they are emerging as important keepers of soil carbon. Plants send them an estimated 5 to 20% of the carbon they take up. In some ecosystems the fungal biomass rivals that of fine roots. It also turns over quickly, and in some places it is the main route by which living carbon enters the soil carbon pool. The two main groups, arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi, belong to separate evolutionary lines and often act in very different ways. Researchers therefore weigh the evidence for each separately. Their effect on dead roots is mixed. Ectomycorrhizal fungi speed fine root decay in some ecosystems but slow it in the roots of Pinus edulis.

soil-env-169.title: Rewetting wetlands to keep their carbon locked away
soil-env-169.text: Peatland covers just 3% of the land surface, yet it stores up to 550 gigatonnes of carbon, 42% of all soil carbon. Wetland restoration aims to keep such places sequestering carbon and storing water. It offers moderate to great mitigation potential on limited land, with low trade-offs and costs, and wetlands store about 45 million tonnes of carbon a year. Peatlands are threatened by drainage for farming, by logging and by peat sales for compost. Blocking the drainage channels lets natural vegetation recover. The gain has a catch: some wetlands are significant sources of methane, and some also emit nitrous oxide.

soil-env-157.title: How thaw lets ancient Arctic carbon escape
soil-env-157.text: Some Arctic carbon has sat frozen for decades, some for millennia. Warming is setting it loose. As the Arctic heats up, the active layer, the soil that thaws each summer, grows deeper. That exposes long-stored carbon to microbes, whose decomposition releases it into the air. Warming also intensifies the Arctic water cycle, and more warm rain deepens the thaw further. The amount that escapes depends on four things. They are how deep the thaw goes, the carbon content of the thawed soil, physical changes to the ground, and the activity of microbes and plants. The change lasts. Once thawed, ground will not return to permafrost for centuries, even if warming reverses. Whether the region already gives off more than it takes in is contested. A 1993 study found the tundra had been a carbon sink until the late 1970s and a net carbon source since. The 2019 Arctic Report Card estimated a net release of 0.3 to 0.6 Pg C a year. Winter emissions, it found, exceeded what vegetation takes up in the growing season. But a 2022 study of atmospheric records from 1980 to 2017 found permafrost regions had been gaining carbon on net. The form of the carbon matters too. Methane lasts under 12 years in the air but warms around 80 times more than CO2 over 20 years. So which gas escapes matters as much as how much carbon.

soil-env-140.title: The permafrost carbon feedback: thaw that feeds itself
soil-env-140.text: Northern circumpolar permafrost holds organic matter equal to 1400–1650 billion tons of carbon, about twice the carbon in the atmosphere. Most of it, ~1,035 billion tons, lies in near-surface permafrost no deeper than 3 metres. When thaw releases that carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, the extra warming drives more thaw. This loop is the permafrost carbon feedback, a northern case of {{ref:soil-env-114}}. Where thawed soil has air, microbes respire the carbon as CO2; where it lacks air, they make methane. Methane will be a small share of the carbon, yet it is expected to cause 40–70% of this century's warming from thaw. Only a fraction of the store will escape. Even under the RCP8.5 scenario of over 4 °C warming, about 5% to 15% of permafrost carbon is expected to be lost over decades and centuries. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases equal to 14–175 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide per 1 °C of warming. Arctic greening will offset some emissions, but very unlikely all of them, and more Arctic wildfires can speed the release. There is widespread agreement that permafrost emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small to cause runaway warming. Gradual thaw would add around 0.09 °C by 2100 if warming is held to 2 °C. Abrupt collapse near 4 °C of warming could add 0.2–0.4 °C. Whether thaw is a global tipping point is debated. Locally it perpetuates itself, but taken together it proceeds gradually with warming.

soil-env-156.title: Counting the carbon locked in frozen soils
soil-env-156.text: In 2003 Tarnocai and colleagues tallied the carbon in cryosols, soils with permafrost within two meters of the surface, using the Northern and Mid Latitudes Soil Database. Later estimates more than doubled the carbon previously known in permafrost soils. Soil organic carbon in the northern circumpolar permafrost region now stands at around 1,460–1,600 Pg, more than twice the carbon in the atmosphere. Much of it sits within reach of thaw. The top 0–30 cm holds about 200 Pg, the top 0–100 cm about 500 Pg and the top 0–300 cm about 1024 Pg. Yedoma, with 400 Pg, and Arctic deltaic deposits, with 240 Pg, add more, generally deeper than the 3 m of traditional studies. Include the Tibetan Plateau, and Northern Hemisphere permafrost holds around 1832 Gt.

soil-env-150.title: Taliks, the ground that never freezes in permafrost country
soil-env-150.text: Even in permafrost country, some ground stays soft all winter. A talik is a zone that remains unfrozen all year within a permafrost area. In continuous permafrost, taliks often lie under shallow lakes in thaw hollows, described in {{ref:soil-env-153}}, and under rivers whose deep water does not freeze in winter. Taliks come in three kinds. A closed talik is surrounded by permafrost. An open talik opens at the top. A through talik also connects to unfrozen ground below the permafrost. One study suggests open taliks are more widespread in fault zones and near large rivers.

soil-env-166.title: The greenhouse gases that rise from farms and fields
soil-env-166.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Some of that comes directly from rice and livestock farming. Some comes indirectly, when forests and other land are converted to farmland. Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of direct agricultural emissions. What farm soils give off depends on soil type, climate and management. Conservation tillage, precision agriculture, better water use and biochar can cut these emissions and store soil carbon at the same time.

soil-env-163.title: How a warming climate wears down soil fertility
soil-env-163.text: Erosion can strip up to 22% of soil carbon in 50 years, and a warmer world gives it more chances. A more vigorous water cycle brings extreme rainfall, making erosion, compaction and a general decline of the soil more likely. Warmth works below ground too. Warmer soils decompose organic matter faster, lowering soil organic carbon and with it the soil's hold on nutrients and water. Soil microbe populations could rise 40–150%, and warmth would favor certain bacteria, shifting the community's makeup. Extra carbon dioxide would speed plant and microbial growth and slow the soil carbon cycle. It would favor slow-growing, efficient microbes called oligotrophs over copiotrophs, which thrive where food is plentiful.

soil-env-165.title: Rising seas and the rice fields at the shoreline
soil-env-165.text: A one-metre rise in the sea would cover several square kilometres of Vietnam's rice paddies. Rising seas threaten farming mainly by flooding low-lying land, especially in South East Asia, through erosion, submerged shorelines and a saltier water table. Bangladesh, India and Vietnam face major rice losses. The sea also pushes saltwater into freshwater wells, which become unusable once saltwater exceeds 2–3%.

soil-env-164.title: New farmland in the thawing far north
soil-env-164.text: Siberia has warmed by three degrees Celsius on average since 1960, much more than the rest of the world, a 2005 study reported. A 2025 study of Arctic Western Siberia projects more permafrost thaw by 2100 and a northward shift of the permafrost zone's southern boundary. Thawing ground could open new farmland. Reports on Russian agriculture expect fields to extend northward, but they warn of possible productivity losses and greater drought risk. Across the Arctic, farming and forestry are expected to gain new opportunities.

soil-env-153.title: Thermokarst, the hollow land left by melting ground ice
soil-env-153.text: When ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground sags into a jumble of marshy hollows and small hummocks. This terrain is called thermokarst, a name that comes from its resemblance to karst, the pitted landscape of dissolving limestone. It occurs across Arctic areas and, on a smaller scale, in mountains such as the Himalayas and the Swiss Alps. Where permafrost holds over 30% ice by volume, thaw depressions fill with water and become thermokarst lakes. These lakes tend to form and drain in a cycle. Each one warms the ground beneath it, so the permafrost below is shallower, and a talik lies under lakes that are deep enough. The lakes also feed the warming. As permafrost thaws around them it releases methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide, a positive feedback that drives more thaw.

soil-env-147.title: Thaw depth, how far summer reaches into frozen soil
soil-env-147.text: On Ellesmere Island summer thaws the ground only 10 cm deep. At Yakutsk it reaches about 2.5 m, and at Yellowknife 5 meters. Thaw depth is the level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, with frozen soil below. Its maximum over two years is the active layer thickness. Maximum air temperature is the main control, but the ground matters too. Coarse sandy or gravelly parent material conducts heat better, giving active layers up to five times deeper than in loam- or clay-rich material. Vegetation and soil organic matter change bulk density and so thermal conductivity, how well soil carries heat. Thaw depth matters for both ecology and construction.

soil-env-119.title: The soil carbon sponge that drinks the rain
soil-env-119.text: Healthy topsoil weighs about 1 gram/cc. The parent mineral soil beneath it weighs 2.6–3.5 grams/cc. The light, porous, well-aggregated layer is what the Australian scientist Walter Jehne called a soil carbon sponge: soil that soaks up water and holds it well. In his 2017 paper Regenerate Earth he linked soil carbon to a restored water cycle that could cool the planet. Bare soil, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation speed the oxidation of its carbon and shrink the sponge. Fire and flooding harm it too. Afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build it back, and the growing sponge also serves as a carbon sink.

soil-env-171.title: Permafrost that grows upward as the ground builds up
soil-env-171.text: Frozen ground does not only thaw. It can also grow upward. When new material piles onto a site under freezing conditions, the frozen ground rises to take it in. This syngenetic growth is efficient compared with heterogenetic growth, in which cold works down into unfrozen ground of uniform composition. The new layers come from river sediment, debris fallen from hillsides, wind-blown material and lake-bottom deposits. As the surface rises it buries organic and mineral soil, making this one of the two main ways permafrost stores carbon. Ice wedges growing upward into permafrost cracks can count as syngenetic too. Studies draw on the permafrost tunnel near Fairbanks, Alaska.

soil-env-158.title: Carbon dioxide, the main gas from thawing permafrost
soil-env-158.text: Most permafrost soils hold oxygen, so their microbes breathe out carbon dioxide. That gas makes up the overwhelming majority of permafrost and Arctic emissions. Studies from the early 2020s add a twist. In the growing season soil microbes respire mostly modern carbon, but in winter they live on ancient carbon. Researchers debate whether rising emissions come mainly from that old frozen carbon or from faster respiration of fresh plant litter in warmer soils. Plants push back. On thawed ground they root deeper, grow larger and take up more carbon, generally the main counteracting feedback. Wildfires push the other way, burning off the insulating organic mat, warming the soil and deepening the active layer.

soil-env-155.title: Two ways plant carbon ends up frozen underground
soil-env-155.text: Permafrost makes no carbon of its own. Carbon from plants must first enter the soil and then be built into the frozen ground. Two processes do this. In syngenetic growth, wind or river sediment or peat raises the surface, by up to 0.5mm/yr for peat and 0.7mm/yr for sediment, burying carbon into permafrost. In cryoturbation, freeze–thaw cycles mix the soil, most often by frost heaving, and carry surface carbon down until the permafrost takes it in. Storage runs faster when cryoturbation and sediment deposition act together.
